markdown:
## In Plain English

This case asks the Supreme Court to decide how a federal immigration law treats “material support” to a terrorist organization. The legal question is whether that support must help the organization actually carry out terrorism, or whether the law can apply even when the support does not directly advance an actual terrorist act. A regular person should care because the answer could affect how immigration law is applied in cases involving alleged support for terrorist groups.

## The Backstory

The case appears to have started in immigration proceedings. The Supreme Court filings refer to decisions by an Immigration Judge, the Board of Immigration Appeals, and the United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit.

The government, named as Todd Blanche, Attorney General, asked the Supreme Court to review the Fourth Circuit case. The government first asked for extra time to file its request for review, and the Chief Justice granted those requests. The government filed its petition for a writ of certiorari on May 29, 2026.

The other side, Izuchukwu Ozurumba, filed a brief in opposition on August 3, 2026. The government filed a reply on August 18, 2026. The case was then considered by the Justices at conferences on September 28 and October 9, 2026. On October 13, 2026, the Supreme Court granted the petition, meaning the Court agreed to hear the case.

After the Court agreed to hear the case, the parties asked for more time to file their written arguments on the merits. The Court granted that request on November 24, 2026. The government’s main brief is due December 7, 2026, and the respondent’s main brief is due January 13, 2027.

The provided docket and filings do not include the lower court opinions, the full petition, the full opposition brief, or the full merits briefs. So the detailed legal arguments of each side are not fully available from the materials provided.

## What Each Side Argues

- **The government’s side:**  
  The government’s filing frames the central question as whether, under 8 U.S.C. § 1182(a)(3)(B)(iv)(VI), material support to a terrorist organization must advance the organization’s actual commission of terrorism. The government also says that the opinions and decisions from the lower courts and immigration authorities are already included in the appendix to its petition for review. It filed a motion asking the Court to allow it to skip preparing a separate “joint appendix,” saying that no other parts of the record need special attention. The provided materials do not include the government’s full brief on the merits, so its complete arguments are not available.

- **The respondent’s side:**  
  The respondent, Izuchukwu Ozurumba, filed a brief in opposition to the government’s request for Supreme Court review. The provided materials do not include that brief, so we cannot summarize the specific arguments the respondent made. The docket also shows that the respondent’s counsel agreed to the proposed schedule for filing the main briefs. The respondent’s full merits brief is due January 13, 2027, but it is not included in the provided filings.

- **What both sides have agreed on so far:**  
  The government’s extension letter says that counsel for the respondent agreed to the proposed briefing schedule. The respondent also consented to the government’s motion asking the Court to dispense with a joint appendix, according to the motion itself.

## Where the Case Stands

The case is **pending**. The Supreme Court has agreed to hear it, but it has not decided the case.

Here is what has happened on the docket:

- The government asked for extensions of time to file its petition for review.
- The petition for a writ of certiorari was filed on May 29, 2026.
- The respondent’s deadline to respond was extended to August 3, 2026.
- The respondent filed a brief in opposition on August 3, 2026.
- The government filed a reply on August 18, 2026.
- The case was distributed for conference on September 28 and October 9, 2026.
- The Supreme Court granted the petition on October 13, 2026.
- The government filed motions on November 12, 2026, including a motion to dispense with a joint appendix and a motion to extend the time to file merits briefs.
- On November 24, 2026, the Court granted the extension for the merits briefs.
- The government’s brief on the merits is due December 7, 2026.
- The respondent’s brief on the merits is due January 13, 2027.

The docket also notes that filings in this case should be submitted in paper form only, not through the Court’s electronic filing system.

The provided docket does not show that the Court has ruled on the motion to dispense with the joint appendix. It also does not show an oral argument date. The government’s extension letter says the proposed schedule would allow the case to be heard during the Court’s February sitting, but that is not the same as a confirmed argument date.

There is no Supreme Court decision, vote count, or holding in the provided materials.

## Legal Terms Explained

- **Petition for a writ of certiorari:**  
  A request asking the Supreme Court to review a lower court’s decision. The Court does not have to accept every case.

- **Respondent:**  
  The party who is responding to the request for Supreme Court review. In this case, that is Izuchukwu Ozurumba.

- **Brief in opposition:**  
  A written filing asking the Supreme Court not to take the case.

- **Merits:**  
  The actual legal issues in the case, after the Supreme Court has agreed to hear it.

- **Joint appendix:**  
  A collection of important lower court records and opinions that the parties prepare for the Supreme Court. The government asked to skip preparing one because it says the key lower court decisions are already in the appendix to its petition.
